source_text: Πλὴν οὕτως ἡμᾶς ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἑλὼν, καὶ πάντα τρόπον ἐκπεριελθὼν, ἐπειδὴ ἤνυστο αὐτῷ τὸ πλεῖον, καὶ μένειν ἐδόκει. τοὐντεῦθεν, ὥσπερ εἴ τις ἀγαθὸς γεωργὸς γῆν ἀργήν τινα καὶ ἤτοι οὐδὲ εὔγειον οὐδαμῶς, ἀλλά τινα ἁλμυρὰν καὶ κεκαυμένην ὑπόπετρόν τε καὶ ψαφαράν, ἢ οὐ πάντῃ μὲν ἄφορον, οὐ δέ γε ἀφυῆ· ἀλλὰ καὶ πολυφυῆ μὲν, χέρσον δὲ ὅμως καὶ ἠμελημένην, ἀκάνθαις καὶ θάμνοις ἀγρίοις ἐστριφνωμένην καὶ δυσεργῆ· ἢ οἷά τις φυτουργὸς ἀνὴρ φυτὸν, ἤτοι ἄγριον, καὶ καρπῶν ἡμέρων ἄφορον μὲν, οὐ μὴν πάντῃ ἄχρηστον. εἴ τις τέχνῃ τῇ φυτουργικῇ φέρων βλαστὸν ἥμερον ἐμφυτεύσει μέσον σχίσας, εἶτα συμβαλὼν καὶ συνδήσας, ἄχρις ἂν συμβλαστήσαντα ὡς ἂν ἄμφω τρέφηται. οὕτως γὰρ ἂν ἴδοις δένδρον τι συμμιγὲς, καὶ νόθον μὲν, εὔκαρπον δὲ ἐξ ἀκάρπου, καρποὺς ἐλαίας τῆς καλῆς ἐπὶ ῥίζαις ἀναφέρον ἀγρίαις, ἢ ἄγριον μὲν, οὐ μὴν ἄχρηστον ἀνδρὶ τεχνίτῃ φυτουργῷ, ἢ καὶ ἥμερον μὲν, εὔκαρπον δὲ ἄλλως, ἢ ἀπορίᾳ τέχνης πάλιν ἀκλάδευτον καὶ ἄποτον καὶ αὐχμηρὸν πνιγόμενον ὑπὸ τῶν ἐκεῖ πολλῶν καὶ περιττῶν ἐκφυομένων βλαστῶν. τελεοῦσθαι δὲ τῇ βλάστῃ, καὶ φέρειν τὸν καρπὸν ὑπ᾽ ἀλλήλων ἐμποδιζόμενον. τοιούτους τινὰς παραλαβὼν, καὶ τέχνῃ ἑαυτοῦ τῇ γεωργικῇ ἐκπεριιὼν καὶ κατανοῶν οὐ τὰ πᾶσιν ὁρώμενα μόνον καὶ ἐν ἐπιφανείᾳ βλεπόμενα· ἀνορύττων δὲ καὶ τῶν ἐνδοτάτων ἀποπειρώμενος, ἐρωτῶν καὶ προτείνων καὶ ἀποκρινομένων ἀκούων· ἐπεὶ κατενόησέ τι οὐκ ἄχρηστον καὶ ἀνωφελὲς καὶ ἀνήνυτον ἐν ἡμῖν, ἔσκαπτεν, ἀνέστρεφεν, ἐπότιζεν, ἐκίνει πάντα, ἅπασαν προσῆγε τὴν παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ τέχνην καὶ ἐπιμέλειαν, καὶ κατειργάζετο ἡμᾶς. ἀκάνθας μὲν καὶ τριβόλους καὶ πᾶν τὸ τῶν ἀγρίων γένος βοτανῶν ἢ φυτῶν, ὅσον ὑλομανοῦσα ἀνέπεμπε καὶ ἀνεδίδου σεσοβημένη ἡ ψυχὴ ἡμῶν, οἷα δὴ ἄτακτος οὖσα καὶ προπετὴς, πᾶν ἐκκόπτων καὶ ἐξαιρῶν, τοῖς ἐλέγχοις καὶ τῷ κωλύειν, καθαπτόμενος ἡμῶν καὶ μάλα Σωκρατικῶς ἔστιν ὅτε καὶ ὑποσκελίζων τῷ λόγῳ, εἴ πη πάντῃ ἀφηνιάζοντας ἡμᾶς ὥσπερ τινὰς τῶν ἀγρίων ἵππων ἑώρα, σκιρτῶντας ἔξω τῆς ὁδοῦ καὶ πολλὰ ἐκπεριτρέχοντας εἰκῇ, ἕως οὗ πειθοῖ τινι καὶ ἀνάγκῃ ὡς ὑπὸ χαλινῷ τῷ ἐκ στόματος ἡμῶν λόγῳ, ἡσυχίως αὐτῷ κατεστήσατο. δυσχερῶς μὲν ἡμῖν καὶ οὐκ ἀλύπως τὸ πρῶτον, οἷα δὴ ἀήθεσι καὶ κατακολουθεῖν τῷ λόγῳ οὐδέπω μεμελετηκόσι, προσάγων τοὺς παρ᾽ ἑαυτοῦ λόγους. ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἐκκαθαίρων ὅμως, ᾗ ἂν ἐπιτηδείους ἡμᾶς ἐποιήσατο, καὶ εὖ προεσκευάσατο εἰς παραδοχὴν τῶν τῆς ἀληθείας λόγων, τότε δὴ, οἷα εὐκατεργασμένῃ γῇ καὶ ἁπαλῇ, ἑτοίμῃ τε ἀναφύειν τὰ ἐπαχθέντα τῶν σπερμάτων, ἐπέφερεν ἀφειδῶς εὔκαιρον καὶ τὴν τῶν σπερμάτων καταβολὴν ποιούμενος. εὔκαιρον καὶ τὴν λοιπὴν ἐπιμέλειαν ἅπασαν οἰκείως ἕκαστα κατεργαζόμενος, καὶ τοῖς οἰκείοις τοῦ λόγου πᾶν μὲν ὅσον ἀμβλὺ καὶ νόθον τῆς ψυχῆς, ἢ πεφυκυίας οὕτως, ἢ καὶ ὑπὸ τροφῶν περιττῶν τοῦ σώματος, παχυνομένης, παροξύνων καὶ ἐξισχναίνων τοῖς λεπτοῖς τῶν λογικῶν παθημάτων λόγοις καὶ τρόποις, οἳ ἐξ ἁπλουστάτων τῶν πρώτων ἀνειλούμενοι ἐπάλληλοι, καὶ ποικίλως στρεφόμενοι, εἰς ἀμήχανόν τινα καὶ δυσεξέλικτον προΐασι πλοκὴν, ἐξανιστῶντες ἡμᾶς ὥσπερ καθεύδοντας, καὶ ἔχεσθαι ἀεὶ τῶν προκειμένων, μηδαμῶς ὑπολισθαίνοντας μήτε ὑπὸ μήκους, μήτε ὑπὸ λεπτότητος ἐκδιδασκόμενοι.
thought_title: The good farmer clears and grafts the soul
orientation: Like a good farmer, Origen clears and tills the soul and trains it to keep to the question in hand.
pass_a_gloss: Thus having taken us from the beginning and gone round every way, when the greater part had been accomplished by him and [we] seemed to stay; from then, as if some good farmer [with] some idle land, either not fertile at all, but salty and scorched, stony-beneath and crumbling; or not wholly barren nor ungrowing, but even rich-growing, yet fallow and neglected, made hard with thorns and wild bushes and hard to work; or as some planter [with] a plant either wild and barren of cultivated fruits, yet not wholly useless, if someone with the planting art, bringing a cultivated shoot, engrafts it, having split the middle, then joining and binding, until both, having sprouted together, are nourished [print ὡς ἄν; Koetschau ὡς ἕν 'as one']. For thus you would see a mixed tree, and bastard, but fruitful from fruitless, bearing up fruits of the good olive on wild roots; or wild, yet not useless to a skilled planter; or cultivated, but otherwise fruitful, or by lack of art again unpruned, unwatered and parched, choked by the many and superfluous shoots growing out there; and hindered by one another from being perfected in growth and bearing the fruit. Having received some such [as us], and going round with his own farming art and observing not only things seen by all and on the surface, but digging up and testing the innermost things, asking and proposing and hearing those answering; when he perceived something in us not useless and unprofitable and futile, he dug, turned over, watered, moved all, applied all his own art and care, and worked us. Thorns and thistles [Genesis 3:18] and the whole kind of wild herbs or plants which our soul, running riot, sent up and put forth, agitated, being disordered and rash, all cutting out and removing, by refutations and by hindering; laying hold of us and very Socratically sometimes also tripping by the argument, if somewhere he saw us wholly throwing off the rein like some wild horses, leaping outside the road and running about much at random, until by some persuasion and necessity, as under a bridle, the word from our mouth, he settled [us] quietly to himself. Difficult for us and not painless at first, as for unaccustomed ones not yet practiced in following the argument, bringing his own arguments; but yet cleansing. When he made us fit and well prepared for reception of the words of truth, then, as to well-worked and soft ground, ready to grow up the seeds brought on, he applied unsparingly, making the sowing of the seeds timely, timely also all the remaining care, working each thing properly; and with the proper [tools] of reason, all that was dull and bastard of the soul, either being so by nature or thickened by superfluous foods of the body, sharpening and thinning by the fine words and modes of logical affections, which, unrolled one upon another from the simplest first [principles] and turned in varied ways, go forward into an inextricable and hard-to-unwind weaving; rousing us as if sleeping, and being taught always to hold to the matters proposed, in no way slipping away either by length or by fineness.

pass_b_english: So he took hold of us from the beginning in this way and went round us by every means. When the greater part of his aim had been reached and it seemed settled that we would stay, from then on he set to work. He was like a good farmer with a piece of untilled land: either land not fertile at all, but salty and scorched, stony and crumbling; or land not wholly barren, nor lacking in growth, but even rich in growth, and yet fallow and neglected, matted hard with thorns and wild scrub and difficult to work. Or he was like a gardener with a plant that is wild and bears no cultivated fruit, and yet is not wholly useless, if someone skilled in the gardener's art should bring a cultivated shoot and graft it in, splitting the stock down the middle, then joining the two and binding them until they grow together and both are nourished. In this way you might see a mixed tree, a hybrid, but fruitful where it was fruitless, bearing the fruit of the good olive on wild roots. Or it may be a plant that is wild and yet not useless to a skilled gardener; or one that is cultivated and fruitful enough in other ways, but which, for want of skill, has again been left unpruned, unwatered and parched, choked by the many superfluous shoots sprouting there, so that it is hindered, the shoots getting in one another's way, from reaching full growth and bearing its fruit.

Such were we when he took us over. Going round us with his own farmer's skill, he examined not only what is visible to all and seen on the surface, but dug down and probed our innermost parts, asking questions, putting forward propositions, and listening to our answers. Once he had seen in us something not useless, not unprofitable, not beyond working, he dug, he turned the soil, he watered, he stirred everything, he brought to bear all his skill and care, and he cultivated us. The thorns and thistles (Genesis 3:18) and every kind of wild weed or plant that our soul threw up and put forth as it ran wild in its agitation, disordered and rash as it was, he cut down and rooted out entirely by refuting us and holding us back. He took us to task, and sometimes, quite in the manner of Socrates, he tripped us up in argument, whenever he saw us bolting from the rein altogether like wild horses, leaping off the road and running about aimlessly, until by a kind of persuasion and constraint, as with a bridle, the word from our own mouth, he brought us quietly to order under him.

At first this was hard for us and not without pain, since we were unused to it and not yet practiced in following an argument, when he brought his own reasoning to bear on us; but all the same he was cleansing us. When he had made us fit and had prepared us well to receive the words of truth, then at last, as on ground well worked and soft and ready to send up the seeds put into it, he set to work unsparingly, sowing the seed at the right time, and at the right time giving all the rest of his care as well, working each thing in its proper way. With the tools that belong to reason he sharpened and refined whatever in the soul was dull and spurious, whether it was so by nature or had grown thick from too much feeding of the body. He did this by the fine arguments and patterns of logical reasoning, which unwind one after another from the simplest first principles and turn in many ways until they advance into a baffling tangle hard to unravel. They roused us as if from sleep, and we were taught always to hold fast to the question before us, never slipping away from it, whether because of its length or because of its subtlety.
notes: Scripture: 'thorns and thistles' (ἀκάνθας καὶ τριβόλους) is the wording of Genesis 3:18 (LXX), noted by Koetschau; cited. The good olive grafted on wild roots recalls Romans 11:17-24, but Gregory reverses Paul's image (a cultivated shoot on a wild stock) and the wording is not Paul's, so it is left uncited. The bridle of the mouth may recall James 3:3; too loose to cite. 'Quite in the manner of Socrates' refers to Socratic cross-examination. Readings: the print's ὡς ἂν ἄμφω τρέφηται is rendered 'both are nourished' (Koetschau ὡς ἕν, 'as one'); ἐκεῖ ('there', print) is kept, though Koetschau reads εἰκῇ ('at random'); ἡσυχίως (print, adverb) is rendered 'quietly'. Doubtful readings kept and rendered by sense: ὑπόπετρον 'stony'; εὔκαρπον δὲ ἄλλως 'fruitful enough in other ways'; ἀπορίᾳ τέχνης 'for want of skill'; τελεοῦσθαι 'reaching full growth'; σεσοβημένη 'in its agitation'; εὔκαιρον (twice) 'at the right time'; νόθον 'spurious'; προΐασι 'advance'. λογικῶν παθημάτων ('logical affections', print and Koetschau; Bengel conjectured μαθημάτων, 'studies') is rendered 'logical reasoning'. ἐκδιδασκόμενοι (nominative in the print and in Koetschau) is rendered as a new clause, 'we were taught'. The section continues straight into 7.2 in the Greek. Hebrews 6:8 uses the same pair ('thorns and thistles') of land that bears no crop; the citation follows Genesis 3:18, the source of the phrase.
